L1@P0: COHEN FACTORIZATIONS: WEAK FUNCTORIALITY AND
L2@P0: APPLICATIONS
L3@P0: SAEED NASSEH AND SEAN SATHER-WAGSTAFF
L4@P0: To Hans-Bjørn Foxby on the occasion of his sixty-fifth birthday
L5@P0: Abstract. We investigate Cohen factorizations of local ring homomorphisms
L6@P0: from three perspectives. First, we prove a “weak functoriality” result for Cohen
L7@P0: factorizations: certain morphisms of local ring homomorphisms induce morphisms of Cohen factorizations. Second, we use Cohen factorizations to study
L8@P0: the properties of local ring homomorphisms (Gorenstein, Cohen-Macaulay,
L9@P0: etc.) in certain commutative diagrams. Third, we use Cohen factorizations to
L10@P0: investigate the structure of quasi-deformations of local rings, with an eye on
L11@P0: the question of the behavior of CI-dimension in short exact sequences.
L12@P0: 1. Introduction
L13@P0: Convention. Throughout this paper, the term “ring” is short for “commutative
L14@P0: noetherian ring with identity”. A local ring is “complete” when it is complete with
L15@P0: respect to its maximal ideal. Let R, S, and T be rings.
L16@P0: Cohen factorizations were introduced in [9] as tools to study local ring homomorphisms. (See Section 2 for definitions and background material.) The utility
L17@P0: of these factorizations can be seen in their many applications; see, e.g., [3, 4, 6, 7,
L18@P0: 8, 13, 22, 28]. The main point of this construction is that it allows one to study
L19@P0: a local ring homomorphism by replacing it with a surjective one; thus, one can
L20@P0: assume that the target is finitely generated over the source, so one can apply finite
L21@P0: homological algebra techniques.
L22@P0: In Section 3 of this paper, we investigate functorial properties of Cohen factorizations. The main result of this section is the following; its proof is in 3.4.
L23@P0: Example 3.5 shows that the separability assumptions (2) are necessary.

L223@P2: Definition 2.1. Let ϕ: (R, m) → (S, n) be a local ring homomorphism.
L224@P2: (a) The embedding dimension of ϕ is edim(ϕ) = edim(S/mS).
L225@P2: (b) The map ϕ is weakly regular if it is flat and the closed fiber S/mS is regular.
L226@P2: (c) The map ϕ is a weakly Cohen if it is weakly regular, and the induced field
L227@P2: extension R/m → S/n is separable, e.g., if char(R/m) = 0 or R/m is perfect of
L228@P2: positive characteristic.
L229@P2: (d) The map ϕ is Cohen if it is weakly Cohen such that n = mS, that is, it is
L230@P2: weakly Cohen such that the closed fiber is a field.

L444@P5: Definition 2.16. A homologically finite R-complex C is semidualizing for R if the
L445@P5: natural morphism R → RHomR(C, C) is an isomorphism in D(R). A dualizing
L446@P5: complex for R is a semidualizing complex D of finite injective dimension, i.e., such
L447@P5: that D is isomorphic in D(R) to a bounded complex of injective R-modules.

L449@P5: only if it is a homomorphic image of a Gorenstein local ring; one implication is from
L450@P5: Grothendieck and Hartshorne [20], and the other is by Kawasaki [23]. In particular,
L451@P5: a complete local ring has a dualizing complex.
